title: Theory of the CH$_\text{S}^-$ Defect in MoS$_2$ Confirming the Origin of the Quantum Emission
abstract: Establishing the microscopic origin of localized emission in two-dimensional materials through consistent agreement between experiment and theory remains challenging. Recent STM/STS-STML measurements assigned an emission near 1.8 eV in monolayer MoS$_2$/hBN(2L)/graphene to the negatively charged CH$_\mathrm{S}^{-}$ defect. However, a comprehensive theoretical description of this emitter is still lacking. Here, we develop such a description and systematically investigate the photophysical properties of CH$_\mathrm{S}^{-}$ in monolayer MoS$_2$, two bilayer configurations, and a MoS$_2$/hBN heterostructure. The defect retains a similar local geometry and favors a singlet ground state in all four environments, whereas its electronic transition, zero-phonon line, electron-phonon coupling, radiative lifetime, and transition-dipole orientation depend strongly on the surrounding layers. The isolated-monolayer model exhibits substantial structural reorganization and produces a broad, dominant phonon sideband that is inconsistent with experiment. Adding an adjacent layer, either MoS$_2$ or hBN, substantially suppresses the phonon sideband, with only a minor dependence on the defect position in bilayer MoS$_2$. In particular, the MoS$_2$/hBN model yields a weak phonon sideband and closely reproduces the experimental photoluminescence lineshape. Our results thus provide the first theoretical agreement of CH$_\mathrm{S}^{-}$ emission and further reveal the role of adjacent layers in determining the electronic, vibronic, and optical properties of the quantum emitters in two-dimensional materials.
summary: This theoretical study investigates the quantum emission from a $	ext{CH}^-	ext{S}$ defect in $	ext{MoS}_2$ using advanced DFT and PL simulation techniques. By comparing predictions across different host environments (monolayer, bilayer, heterostructure), the authors establish that the $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{hBN}$ interface best reproduces the experimental photoluminescence spectrum. This work clarifies the role of adjacent layers in determining the optical properties of 2D quantum emitters.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of theoretically establishing the microscopic origin of localized quantum emission from the $	ext{CH}^-	ext{S}$ defect in $	ext{MoS}_2$ and related 2D materials.
main_result: The $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{hBN}$ heterostructure model provides the first theoretical agreement by yielding a weak phonon sideband and closely reproducing the experimental photoluminescence lineshape.
method: The study employs first-principles calculations (DFT/HSE06) combined with advanced methods to simulate photoluminescence (PL) spectra using the full-phonon generating-function approach.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{CH}^-	ext{S}$ defect embedded in various environments: monolayer $	ext{MoS}_2$, bilayer $	ext{MoS}_2$, and the $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{hBN}$ heterostructure.
key_observables: Zero-Phonon Line (ZPL) energy, PL spectral lineshape, phonon sideband intensity, radiative lifetime, and transition-dipole orientation.
important_parameters: The dependence of electronic and vibronic properties on the surrounding layers (e.g., the presence of hBN vs. isolated monolayer).
main_assumptions: The isolated-monolayer model is disfavored due to an inconsistent, overly broad phonon sideband; the $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{hBN}$ model is deemed most physically relevant.
figures_summary: Figures compare calculated PL spectra for four different defect environments against experimental data, and show simulated phonon spectral densities for these systems.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares four structural environments ($	ext{CH}^-	ext{S}$ in monolayer, bilayer, and heterostructure) by calculating structural parameters, electronic transitions, and full PL spectra to pinpoint the most accurate physical model.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the quantum optics of solid-state emitters, providing detailed vibronic coupling analysis (Huang-Rhys factors, phonon modes) crucial for understanding energy relaxation in nanoscale quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Optimized geometries of CH− S in each system. a MoS2 monolayer; b MoS2 bilayer with CH− S at the top layer; c MoS2 bilayer with CH− S at the middle layer; d MoS2/hBN heterostructure; and e Zoom-in CH− S defect on the MoS2 layer.

Figure 2. Kohn–Sham electronic transitions at the Γ point for CH− S in MoS2. a Monolayer MoS2. b Bilayer MoS2 with CH− S at the outer/top S site. c Bilayer MoS2 with CH− S at the inner/middle S site. d Heterostructure MoS2/hBN with CH− S . Filled and unfilled arrows denote occupied and unoccupied Kohn–Sham states, respectively, while upward and downward arrows indicate spin-up and spin-down channels. The green arrow marks the electronic transition used to calculate the optical properties.

Figure 3. Comparison of the calculated and experimental PL spectra of CH− S . Calculated spectra are shown for CH− S in monolayer MoS2, the top- and middle-bilayer configurations, and the MoS2/hBN heterostructure, together with the experimental spectrum. The spectra are normalized to their respective maximum intensities, and the calculated ZPL positions are aligned with the experimental emission peak to compare the PL lineshapes and relative PSB contributions independently of the absolute transition energies. Experimental data is adapted with permission from Ref. [30].

Figure 4. Simulated phonon spectral density of CH− S and the most two dominant phonon modes. a Monolayer MoS2. b,c Bilayer MoS2 with CH− S at the outer/top S site and inner/middle S site, respectively. d MoS2/hBN heterostructure with CH− S defect on the MoS2 layer. The red arrow represents the vibrational direction.
